analysis.one_liner: Gives state and local government workers nationwide the legal right to unionize and bargain over pay and working conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with 181 cosponsors, including 8 Republicans, it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on May 16, 2024 and received no hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, whether a firefighter, teacher, nurse, or sanitation worker can form a union and bargain over wages depends entirely on their state — some states guarantee it, some states ban or sharply limit it. This bill sets a national floor: it would require every state to let public employees organize, choose a union, and bargain in good faith, with binding arbitration to settle contract disputes. Where a state's law already meets the standard, the state keeps its own system; where it does not, the Federal Labor Relations Authority would administer bargaining rights for those workers directly. The bill bans strikes and lockouts that would disrupt emergency or public safety services.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local government workers — teachers, firefighters, EMTs, police, sanitation and transit workers — especially the millions in states that currently bar or severely limit public-sector collective bargaining. They would gain a federally enforceable right to form a union, bargain over wages and conditions, have union dues deducted from paychecks, and resolve contract impasses through binding arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public employees in states with weak union rights

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires every state to guarantee public employees the right to self-organize, join or assist a labor organization, bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and act together for mutual aid [S2].
Public employers would be required to recognize a union chosen by a majority of employees, bargain with it, and put any agreement into a written contract or memorandum of understanding [S2].

States that do not meet the federal minimum standards would fall under rules administered by the Federal Labor Relations Authority, which would supervise elections, set bargaining units, resolve complaints, and enforce compliance with court-backed orders [S2].
The bill requires payroll deduction of union fees for employees who choose it, a mechanism some states prohibit [S2].

An interest impasse resolution mechanism — such as mediation, fact-finding, or arbitration culminating in a binding resolution — would give workers a way to settle contracts even where strikes are barred [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, and ultimately their taxpayers, who would face new collective bargaining obligations — potentially higher wages, benefits, and administrative costs — plus the cost of complying with or litigating federal determinations. States with no public-sector bargaining laws would lose their current legal regime for these workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans strikes, lockouts, and other job actions by emergency services employees and law enforcement officers when they would disrupt emergency or public safety services, so workers in those jobs would gain bargaining rights but not the ability to strike [S2].

Binding resolution of contract impasses could raise costs for state and local governments, which are funded by taxpayers, and the bill authorizes appropriations to carry it out without setting an amount [S2].

The bill overrides state policy choices: in states whose laws fall short, the Federal Labor Relations Authority would administer bargaining rights for covered workers, reducing state control over public employment terms [S2].

Exemptions mean it would not reach small political subdivisions (under 5,000 people or fewer than 25 employees, where the state opts them out), state militia or National Guard employees, or require bargaining over pension or retirement benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would extend enforceable union and bargaining rights to a large group of workers who currently have none, which is its main and clear benefit. The trade-offs are real: it shifts authority over public employment from states to a federal agency in non-complying states, could raise government labor costs borne by taxpayers, and deliberately withholds the right to strike from police and emergency workers — leaving them to rely on binding arbitration instead. States already meeting the standards would see little change, since the bill does not preempt their laws.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it sat there until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 16, 2024 by Rep. Matt Cartwright (D-PA) with an initial group of cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1].
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote appear in the bill's action history, which ends with the referral [S4].
The bill ended the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 without ever reaching the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments in states that restrict public-sector bargaining keep their current legal regime, and no federal bargaining rights take effect for those workers.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled an initial list of 90+ cosponsors from both parties on introduction day.

for.name: 181 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on to the bill, giving it broad stated support — though not enough action to move it out of committee.

for.name: Public-sector labor organizations
for.role: Intended beneficiaries of the bill's bargaining rights
for.what_they_did: The bill was drafted to expand their members' rights and requires payroll deduction of union fees; their advocacy for the measure is widely reported.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it remained in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 173 of 181 cosponsors — with 8 Republicans, including Reps. Fitzpatrick (PA), Bacon (NE), Chavez-DeRemer (OR), Lawler (NY), and Molinaro (NY) [S2][S3]; the committee that declined to act was Republican-controlled.

industries.note: The bill would give unions new members in states that currently bar public-sector bargaining and guarantees payroll deduction of dues, materially growing their base and revenue. Workers would gain enforceable bargaining rights alongside.

Governments would be required to recognize unions, bargain in good faith, and submit to binding impasse resolution, which can raise labor costs funded by taxpayers. States with restrictive bargaining laws would lose control over these terms to a federal agency.
